claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are caused by facile dislocation glide in a single-phase disordered solid solution.
The CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has low lattice friction or a low Peierls barrier.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state contains minimal short-range order and few nanoscale precipitate obstacles.
Dislocation-mediated deformation with few obstacles produces favorable plasticity and machinability at the expense of yield strength and hardness.
The applicable starting composition is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The applicable starting structure is a chemically disordered, single-phase solid solution that is likely FCC and lacks secondary phases or significant short-range order.
Controlled aging can form coherent nanoscale Ti-rich or related precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi without changing grain size or the overall phase.
Nanoscale precipitates or short-range order act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Scarcity of precipitates or short-range order in the as-cast state permits easy dislocation motion.
A uniform, chemically disordered lattice permits dislocations to nucleate and move with little hindrance.
Facile dislocation motion in the starting state results in low work hardening.
Aging-induced precipitates increase dislocation pinning through obstacle hardening and thereby raise yield strength and hardness.
The availability of effective dislocation barriers controls the observed strength-plasticity-machinability trade-off.
The aged alloy will have significantly higher hardness and yield strength than the starting as-cast alloy.
The aged alloy will likely have lower ductility than the starting alloy.
Microscopy of the aged alloy should reveal coherent nanoscale precipitates interacting with and impeding dislocations.
The proposed mechanism applies only while CoCrFeNiTi retains a simple solid-solution matrix without large-scale phase separation or deleterious intermetallic formation.
From room temperature to moderate temperatures and at standard strain rates, dislocation glide is the dominant deformation mechanism in the specified CoCrFeNiTi state.

contradictions.description: The intervention is intended to create precipitates while also being described as not altering the overall phase and as retaining a simple solid solution. Formation of a distinct precipitate phase ordinarily makes the material multiphase unless 'overall phase' is intended to refer only to retention of the matrix phase.

The rule treats both failure to form precipitates and failure to strengthen as falsification. If aging does not form the intended precipitates, however, the mediator was not successfully manipulated, so unchanged strength does not decisively test the proposed obstacle-hardening mechanism.
